variants.title: Promote on evidence
variants.context: Evidence promotes a model in five stages: lock the evaluation contract before training, test offline behavior against the production baseline, observe in shadow without authority, limit real exposure with a canary, then decide and keep watching the same slices.
variants.prompt: A team is preparing a new ranking model for release. Put the promotion stages in order.

items.text: Promote only when quality and guardrails pass, then keep the same cohort and slice checks running afterwards.
Measure holdout quality, uncertainty, invariants, robustness, and latency against the model currently in production.
Name the population, split unit, primary metric, guardrails, minimum detectable effect, and failure slices before comparing candidates.
Run the candidate on production inputs without changing user outcomes, checking feature compatibility, stability, and cost.
Send a small representative traffic slice to the candidate with automatic rollback conditions and comparable outcome logging.

variants.hint: One stage happens before any candidate exists at all.
variants.explanation: The evaluation contract is locked first so that the metric, guardrails, and slices cannot be chosen after the results are visible.

variants.title: Promote on evidence
variants.context: Evidence promotes a model in five stages: lock the evaluation contract before training, test offline behavior against the production baseline, observe in shadow without authority, limit real exposure with a canary, then decide and keep watching the same slices.
variants.prompt: A fraud classifier is being replaced. Put the promotion stages in order.

items.text: Score the sealed holdout weeks, report the spread across seeds, and compare with the deployed model.
Agree in advance that the primary metric is recall at a fixed review capacity, with latency and appeal rate as guardrails.
Give the candidate two percent of authorizations with a rollback trigger on the appeal rate.
Promote it and keep the same slices, cohorts, and guardrails reporting after launch.
Mirror live authorizations into the candidate while the deployed model still decides every payment.

variants.hint: Deciding what counts as better is itself one of the stages.
variants.explanation: Naming the metric and guardrails before the comparison is what stops a losing candidate from being rescued by a metric chosen later.

variants.title: Promote on evidence
variants.context: Evidence promotes a model in five stages: lock the evaluation contract before training, test offline behavior against the production baseline, observe in shadow without authority, limit real exposure with a canary, then decide and keep watching the same slices.
variants.prompt: A generated summary feature is getting a new model. Put the promotion stages in order.

items.text: Run the offline suite for task success, factuality, and latency against the model in production.
Expose one small cohort with logging comparable to the baseline and an automatic rollback trigger.
Decide from the predeclared criteria, then keep the slice and safety reports running after promotion.
Shadow real requests and store the candidate outputs for review without showing them to anyone.
Write the contract first: the population, what counts as task success, the human review budget, and the safety guardrails.

variants.hint: Generated output changes what you measure, not the order you measure it in.
variants.explanation: The stages are the same for generation, because automated similarity scores rarely establish usefulness without shadow and cohort evidence.

variants.title: Build an evaluation that cannot leak
variants.context: Reliable offline evaluation avoids contamination: choose the split unit and boundary first, fit every transformation on training data only, then measure, and keep the final holdout untouched until the promotion decision.
variants.prompt: A demand forecast is being evaluated on two years of history. Put the setup steps in order.

items.text: Score the next forward window without refitting anything on it.
Set the split boundary by event time so every evaluation window falls after its training window.
Fit scaling, encoding, and imputation on the training window only.
Roll the window forward and report quality across seasons and forecast horizons.

variants.hint: Anything fitted on data the model should not have seen is already leakage.
variants.explanation: Temporal splits and transformations fitted only on the past are what keep a backtest from importing future information.

variants.title: Build an evaluation that cannot leak
variants.context: Reliable offline evaluation avoids contamination: choose the split unit and boundary first, fit every transformation on training data only, then measure, and keep the final holdout untouched until the promotion decision.
variants.prompt: A churn model has many rows per account. Put the setup steps in order.

items.text: Leave the final holdout untouched until the promotion decision.
Assign every row belonging to an account to exactly one split.
Measure the holdout and confirm important subgroups are represented in it.
Pick the unit that could leak across examples, which here is the account rather than the individual row.
Fit the transformations on the training split alone.

variants.hint: The split unit is chosen before anything is split.
variants.explanation: Splitting by the leaking unit first is what makes the holdout an estimate of unseen accounts rather than of memorized ones.

variants.title: Build an evaluation that cannot leak
variants.context: Reliable offline evaluation avoids contamination: choose the split unit and boundary first, fit every transformation on training data only, then measure, and keep the final holdout untouched until the promotion decision.
variants.prompt: A search ranker is evaluated on logged clicks. Put the setup steps in order.

items.text: Run several seeds and report the spread instead of a single point estimate.
Group examples by query so every candidate for one request stays in the same split.
Compute NDCG within each query group rather than over the pooled rows.
Correct for position and exposure bias before treating logged clicks as relevance labels.

variants.hint: Clicks are not relevance until something has been corrected.
variants.explanation: Ranking is evaluated within request groups, and biased click labels have to be corrected before they can stand in for relevance.

variants.title: Cost the operating point
variants.context: A threshold turns a continuous score into an action, so operating points are compared by expected error cost: false positives times the cost of a false positive plus false negatives times the cost of a miss.
variants.prompt: In a fraud review setting a false positive costs 8 and a missed fraud costs 120. At the current threshold a week produces 300 false positives and 12 missed fraud cases. What is the expected error cost for that week?
variants.hint: Each error type is counted at its own price before anything is added.
variants.explanation: 300 false positives at 8 is 2400, 12 misses at 120 is 1440, and the operating point therefore costs 3840.

mistakes.feedback: That swaps the two costs, pricing false positives at 120 and misses at 8.
That counts only the false positives and leaves the missed fraud out of the total.

variants.title: Cost the operating point
variants.context: A threshold turns a continuous score into an action, so operating points are compared by expected error cost: false positives times the cost of a false positive plus false negatives times the cost of a miss.
variants.prompt: For churn outreach a false positive costs 2 and a missed churner costs 18. Threshold A produces 900 false positives and 40 misses. Threshold B produces 1500 false positives and 15 misses. How much lower is the expected error cost of the cheaper threshold?
variants.hint: Price each threshold on its own, then compare the two totals.
variants.explanation: Threshold A costs 1800 plus 720, which is 2520, and threshold B costs 3000 plus 270, which is 3270, so A is cheaper by 750.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts raw counts, 600 extra reviews minus 25 fewer misses, instead of costs.
That adds the two totals rather than comparing them.

variants.title: Cost the operating point
variants.context: A threshold turns a continuous score into an action, so operating points are compared by expected error cost: false positives times the cost of a false positive plus false negatives times the cost of a miss.
variants.prompt: In an abuse moderation queue a false positive costs 4 and a missed violation costs 55. A day produces 200 false positives and 30 missed violations. What is the expected error cost for that day?
variants.hint: The cheaper error can still dominate if it happens often enough, so price both.
variants.explanation: 200 false positives at 4 is 800, 30 misses at 55 is 1650, and the day therefore costs 2450.

mistakes.feedback: That swaps the two costs, pricing false positives at 55 and misses at 4.
That adds the two error counts and ignores their very different costs.

variants.title: Grant the authority the evidence earned
variants.context: Offline improvement is necessary but not sufficient. Match the authority granted to a candidate to the evidence it has actually earned, and keep guardrails able to block a promotion that the primary metric would wave through.
variants.prompt: A candidate lifts the primary metric by 2.4 percent, moves no guardrail the wrong way, and adds 7 percent latency that stays inside budget. Shadow has already confirmed feature parity. What is the right next step?
options: Hold it in shadow until the measured lift doubles, because 2.4 percent is a small gain.
Give it a canary cohort with predeclared rollback conditions and comparable outcome logging.
Promote it to all traffic now, since the shadow run and the offline evidence already agree.
optionFeedback: Wrong. The contract declared a minimum detectable effect in advance, so raising the bar afterwards is not a gate.
Correct. Shadow evidence supports bounded real authority next, which is exactly what a canary grants.
Wrong. Shadow runs carry no user outcomes, so full traffic skips the only stage that measures real impact under rollback.
variants.hint: Which stage has this candidate not yet passed?
variants.explanation: Authority increases one stage at a time, and a clean shadow run is the evidence that justifies a bounded cohort rather than full traffic.

variants.title: Grant the authority the evidence earned
variants.context: Offline improvement is necessary but not sufficient. Match the authority granted to a candidate to the evidence it has actually earned, and keep guardrails able to block a promotion that the primary metric would wave through.
variants.prompt: A candidate wins offline quality by 4.6 percent and keeps every slice healthy, but it consumes 34 percent more latency and pushes p99 past the decision deadline. What should the gate do?
options: Canary it at one percent, since a small cohort keeps the latency risk contained anyway.
Block promotion and treat the latency budget as a guardrail a quality win cannot buy.
Promote it and raise the latency budget, because users notice quality more than milliseconds.
optionFeedback: Wrong. A canary tests unknowns, and this candidate already fails a guardrail that was measured offline.
Correct. Guardrails exist to block promotions that the primary quality score would otherwise wave through.
Wrong. Rewriting the budget to fit the candidate removes the constraint instead of satisfying it.
variants.hint: A guardrail is not a tiebreaker to be weighed against the primary metric.
variants.explanation: Latency, reliability, fairness, and business constraints can block promotion even when the primary quality score improves.

variants.title: Grant the authority the evidence earned
variants.context: Offline improvement is necessary but not sufficient. Match the authority granted to a candidate to the evidence it has actually earned, and keep guardrails able to block a promotion that the primary metric would wave through.
variants.prompt: A canary shows a 0.3 percent lift whose confidence interval still includes zero at the current sample size, and no guardrail has moved. What is the appropriate decision?
options: Promote it, because the point estimate is positive and nothing has regressed so far.
Roll it back, because a lift that is not yet significant should be read as a regression.
Keep the canary running until the sample reaches the predeclared power, then decide.
optionFeedback: Wrong. An interval that includes zero cannot separate a real lift from noise, so the evidence does not yet support promotion.
Wrong. Failing to reach significance is not evidence of harm, and no guardrail has moved.
Correct. The minimum detectable effect and power were declared in advance, so the answer is more evidence.
variants.hint: Ask what the interval says, not what the point estimate says.
variants.explanation: Power analysis is part of the evaluation contract, so an underpowered result calls for more exposure time rather than a decision either way.

variants.title: Name the pitfall behind the score
variants.context: Optimistic scores usually come from four pitfalls: data leakage, selection bias, metric gaming, and multiple testing. Each one has its own correction, so naming the right one matters.
variants.prompt: Offline quality is excellent and production quality is far worse. The team finds that one feature was standardized using statistics from the whole dataset and another is derived from a field written after the outcome. Which pitfall is this?
options: Selection bias: the test set did not represent production users and conditions.
Multiple testing: enough repeated comparisons eventually produce a false positive.
Data leakage: split by time and fit every transformation on training data only.
optionFeedback: Wrong. The problem is not who is in the test set but what those rows were allowed to know.
Wrong. Nothing here describes many repeated comparisons producing one lucky winner.
Correct. Future or target derived information reached the inputs, which is exactly what leakage means.
variants.hint: Ask what the training inputs were able to see.
variants.explanation: Leakage inflates offline scores and disappears in production, so temporal splits and training only transformations are the correction.

variants.title: Name the pitfall behind the score
variants.context: Optimistic scores usually come from four pitfalls: data leakage, selection bias, metric gaming, and multiple testing. Each one has its own correction, so naming the right one matters.
variants.prompt: A team ran 30 model variants over a quarter and shipped the first one that reached a p value below 0.05, with no decision criterion declared beforehand. Which pitfall is this?
options: Data leakage: future information entered the model inputs during training.
Metric gaming: the proxy metric improved without any matching business value.
Multiple testing: predeclare criteria and correct with Bonferroni or false discovery rate control.
optionFeedback: Wrong. The inputs are not implicated here; the search over variants is.
Wrong. Nothing says the metric was the wrong one, only that it was tested many times over.
Correct. Repeated experiments eventually produce a false positive, which is why criteria are declared in advance.
variants.hint: Count how many chances the team gave itself to see a win.
variants.explanation: Repeated comparisons need predeclared criteria and a correction, otherwise the winner is often just the luckiest of many tries.

variants.title: Name the pitfall behind the score
variants.context: Optimistic scores usually come from four pitfalls: data leakage, selection bias, metric gaming, and multiple testing. Each one has its own correction, so naming the right one matters.
variants.prompt: A new ranker raises click through rate on the recommended row by 6 percent, while subscriptions stay flat and unsubscribes rise. Which pitfall is this?
options: Multiple testing: one comparison among many came out positive purely by chance.
Metric gaming: the proxy improved without improving value, so validate against business KPIs.
Selection bias: the evaluated traffic did not represent real deployment conditions.
optionFeedback: Wrong. A single consistent result with a matching negative signal is not a chance finding.
Correct. Optimization improved a proxy while the outcomes the business cares about did not move.
Wrong. The measurement covered real traffic, and the problem is what was measured rather than who was measured.
variants.hint: Compare what improved with what the product is actually for.
variants.explanation: A proxy can rise while value does not, so important launches are validated against business KPIs and not only the primary score.
